text: Titanoboa was a giant snake that lived about 60 million years ago in what is now Colombia, in northern South America. Scientists estimate it was about 13 m long and weighed around 1,100 kg.

That makes it longer than a typical school bus and heavier than a small car. Its body was so thick that at its widest, it would have reached up past a grown-up's waist. It is the biggest snake ever found, though a newer discovery from India may rival it.

st.prompt: How did scientists work out Titanoboa's length when they had no complete skeleton?

options.t: By comparing the size of its backbones with those of living snakes
By measuring the length of its fossil footprints
By counting the rings in its teeth

st.reveal: Snakes have hundreds of backbones, called vertebrae. Scientists compared the size and shape of Titanoboa's vertebrae with those of living boas and anacondas, and worked out how long a snake with bones that big would be.

n.certNote: Titanoboa's size is estimated from its backbones, since no complete skeleton or skull-to-tail fossil has been found. Most estimates give about 13 m and over a tonne, but the exact figures could be somewhat higher or lower. Its link to ancient temperatures is also debated.

d.try: Measure Titanoboa. Take a ball of string and measure out 13 m along a corridor, playground or garden, with an adult's help. Lie down next to it and see how many of you would fit end to end. Then mark 7.7 m, the length of the longest snake ever measured in captivity.
myth: Titanoboa lived alongside the dinosaurs and hunted them.
Titanoboa appeared a few million years after the big dinosaurs died out, about 66 million years ago. It never met a T. rex. It mostly ate fish, and perhaps crocodile relatives.
facts: Cerrejón coal mine, northern Colombia, described in 2009

sec.t:
Titanoboa's bones were found in the Cerrejón coal mine, one of the world's largest open-pit mines. Huge machines dig out coal there from rocks that formed in an ancient swampy rainforest.

In the early 2000s, scientists exploring the mine found [[fossil|fossils]] of giant turtles, crocodile relatives and fish. Among them were snake backbones far larger than those of any living snake. In 2009, a team announced the new giant in the journal *Nature*. They named it *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*, "titanic boa from Cerrejón".

A snake's body is mostly a long chain of backbones, called vertebrae, with ribs attached. Titanoboa's vertebrae were each about as wide as a man's hand stretched out.

By comparing them with the vertebrae of living boas and anacondas, scientists worked out how long and heavy the whole snake must have been. Because they had bones from many individuals, they could estimate the biggest ones well, though the numbers are still estimates.

The longest snake ever measured in captivity is a reticulated python called Medusa, at about 7.7 m. Titanoboa was almost twice as long.

{{story:fossils-form}}

Titanoboa lived after the dinosaurs had gone. The world was warm, and much of northern South America was covered in steamy rainforest with wide rivers and swamps, a bit like the [[@brazil-amazon|Amazon]] today.

Like modern anacondas, it probably spent much of its time in water, which helped support its enormous weight. It was likely an ambush hunter, lying still and then grabbing prey. Its main food was probably fish, including lungfish more than 2 m long. It may also have caught crocodile relatives.

Titanoboa wasn't venomous. Like boas and pythons, it would have killed by squeezing.

Snakes are cold-blooded. Their bodies take the temperature of their surroundings, so very big snakes need warm places to stay active. The 2009 team suggested that, to grow so large, Titanoboa needed average temperatures of about 30 to 34°C, hotter than [[tropical|tropical]] South America today.

Other scientists argued that body size alone can't tell us the temperature so precisely. This debate is still going on.

In 2024, scientists from IIT Roorkee described another huge snake, found in a lignite mine at Panandhro in Kutch, Gujarat. It lived about 47 million years ago. They named it *Vasuki indicus*, after Vasuki, the king of serpents in Hindu stories, who was wrapped around a mountain as a rope when gods and demons churned the ocean.

Based on its vertebrae, it may have been between about 11 and 15 m long. That could make it as long as Titanoboa, or even longer. It belonged to a different family of snakes, now [[extinct|extinct]], and may have spread from India to Africa and Europe.

No snake today comes close to these sizes. Snakes are still among the most surprising animals around, from pythons to India's own [[@king-cobra|king cobra]], which can grow over 5 m. Long before Titanoboa, the swamps of the world were ruled by another kind of giant, as the story of the [[@lost-giant-insects|giant insects]] shows.

text: Sabre-toothed cats like Smilodon probably used their long fangs for a precise killing bite, not for stabbing wildly or crushing bone. They first pinned their prey down with powerful front legs and a thick neck. Then they opened their jaws very wide and drove the fangs into the soft throat.

The fangs were long but fairly thin and could snap. So the strategy was "grab first, bite carefully". Computer models show Smilodon's jaw muscles were weaker than a lion's, but its neck and shoulders were very strong.

st.prompt: Smilodon's long fangs were quite thin. What was the danger of using them the wrong way?

options.t: They could snap if they hit bone or the prey struggled
They could fall out every time it yawned

st.reveal: The sabres were long and flattened from side to side, like a knife blade. Great for a deep, precise bite into soft flesh, but risky against bone or a twisting animal. Scientists think Smilodon held prey still with its strong front legs first, then bit.

sec.h: A cat built like a wrestler
sec.t:
The best-known sabre-toothed cat is Smilodon, which lived in the Americas during the [[@ice-ages|ice ages]]. The largest [[species|species]], from South America, may have weighed up to about 400 kg, heavier than most tigers. It had a short tail, long powerful front legs and a body built more for strength than speed.

Its upper fangs could reach about 28 cm long, including the part buried in the jaw. That is longer than a big banana. They were flattened from side to side, with fine serrations along the edge in young adults, like a steak knife. Like [[@teeth|your own teeth]], they came in two sets. Young Smilodon had milk sabres first, and for a while the adult sabres grew in beside them, so a youngster could have four long fangs at once.

The best place in the world to study Smilodon is the [[@la-brea|La Brea Tar Pits]] in [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]]. Sticky tar oozed up through the ground there for thousands of years. Big plant-eaters got stuck, and meat-eaters that came to eat them got stuck too. Scientists have dug up the bones of thousands of Smilodon from the pits.

Some of these skeletons show old injuries that had healed, such as damaged hips or legs. A badly injured hunter could not easily feed itself. Some scientists think this means Smilodon lived in groups and shared food, like lions. Others think the injured cats simply scavenged. Smilodon is now the state [[fossil|fossil]] of California.

Long sabre-like teeth [[evolve|evolved]] more than once. Several different groups of meat-eating [[mammal|mammals]] grew them, including a South American relative of marsupials that was not a cat at all. Sabre-toothed cats also lived in Africa, Europe and Asia. Their fossils have been found in the Siwalik Hills, along the foot of the Himalayas in India.

Smilodon died out about 10,000 years ago, at around the same time as [[@mammoths|mammoths]], [[@giant-sloths|giant sloths]] and many other [[@ice-age-animals|big ice age animals]] in the Americas. The [[climate|climate]] was warming, and humans had arrived and were hunting the same large prey. Scientists still debate how much each mattered. Without big, slow animals to hold down, a cat built like a wrestler had little to eat.

text: ब्लड फ़ॉल्स, यानी "ख़ूनी झरना", [[@antarctica|अंटार्कटिका]] के टेलर हिमनद के सिरे से बहता एक लाल-नारंगी धब्बा है। बर्फ़ के बहुत नीचे पानी साफ़ होता है। वह बेहद खारा होता है और उसमें ढेर सारा लोहा घुला होता है। जब वह रिसकर बाहर आता है और हवा से मिलता है, तो लोहा ऑक्सीजन से मिलकर लाल हो जाता है। यही रसायन [[@rust|ज़ंग]] भी बनाता है।

यह पानी हिमनद के नीचे बंद खारे पानी के एक प्राचीन तालाब से आता है, जो शायद 10 लाख साल से भी ज़्यादा समय से वहाँ क़ैद है। इससे भी अजीब बात यह है कि इसमें नन्हे [[microbe|सूक्ष्मजीव]] रहते हैं, घुप अँधेरे में और लगभग बिना ऑक्सीजन के। वैज्ञानिक इनका अध्ययन यह समझने के लिए करते हैं कि दूसरी दुनियाओं में जीवन कैसे बच सकता है।

sec.t:
1911 में ऑस्ट्रेलियाई भूवैज्ञानिक ग्रिफ़िथ टेलर रॉबर्ट फ़ॉल्कन स्कॉट के ब्रिटिश [[expedition|अभियान]] के साथ इस इलाके की खोज कर रहे थे। उन्हें एक हिमनद मिला, जिसके सिरे पर एक लाल, जमा हुआ झरना था। बाद में इस हिमनद का नाम उन्हीं के नाम पर पड़ा।

टेलर और दूसरों ने अंदाज़ा लगाया कि यह रंग लाल [[algae|शैवाल]] से आता है, यानी पौधों जैसे नन्हे जीव जो कभी-कभी बर्फ़ को गुलाबी रँग देते हैं। यह अंदाज़ा ग़लत था, पर इसे साबित करने में दशकों का शोध लगा। लाल पानी के स्रोत का पूरा नक्शा वैज्ञानिक 21वीं सदी में जाकर बना पाए।

बहुत पहले, जब समुद्र का स्तर ऊँचा था, समुद्री पानी इस घाटी में भर गया था। बाद में [[@glaciers|हिमनद]] इसके ऊपर बढ़ आया और उस खारे पानी के एक तालाब को नीचे फँसा लिया। समय के साथ कुछ पानी जम गया, जिससे बचा हुआ पानी और भी खारा हो गया।

इस खारे पानी ने नीचे की चट्टान से लोहा भी उठा लिया। बर्फ़ के नीचे हवा नहीं थी, इसलिए लोहा घुला रहा और पानी साफ़ रहा। नमक पानी के जमने का तापमान घटा देता है, इसलिए यह खारा पानी लगभग −7 °C पर भी तरल रहता है। जब यह हिमनद के अगले हिस्से की दरारों से निचुड़कर बाहर आता है, तो पहली बार ऑक्सीजन से मिलता है। लोहे का [[oxidation|ऑक्सीकरण]] होता है, और पल भर में पानी ज़ंग जैसा लाल होने लगता है।

2023 में जॉन्स हॉपकिन्स यूनिवर्सिटी के वैज्ञानिकों ने इन लाल ठोस कणों को ताकतवर सूक्ष्मदर्शियों से देखा। उन्हें लोहे से भरे नन्हे गोल दाने मिले, लाल रक्त कोशिका से भी कहीं छोटे। ये नैनोस्फ़ियर, न कि साधारण क्रिस्टल, झरने को उसका रंग देते हैं।

इसीलिए ब्लड फ़ॉल्स अंतरिक्ष वैज्ञानिकों को रोमांचित करता है। बृहस्पति के चाँद [[@europa|यूरोपा]] और शनि के चाँद एनसेलेडस पर मोटी बर्फ़ के नीचे खारे पानी के समुद्र हैं। मंगल पर भी नमक और बर्फ़ है। अगर सूक्ष्मजीव अंटार्कटिका के एक हिमनद के नीचे जी सकते हैं, तो शायद वहाँ भी कुछ ऐसा ही बचा रह सकता हो।

लोहे के नन्हे दाने भी मायने रखते हैं। खनिज खोजता मंगल का कोई रोवर इन नैनोस्फ़ियर को चूक सकता है, क्योंकि ये साधारण क्रिस्टल नहीं हैं। वैज्ञानिकों का मानना है कि आगे के अभियानों को इन्हें खोजने के औज़ार चाहिए।

sec.h: धरती की सबसे सूखी जगहों में से एक
sec.t:
मैकमर्डो ड्राई वैलीज़, जहाँ ब्लड फ़ॉल्स है, धरती की [[@extreme-driest|सबसे सूखी]] जगहों में गिनी जाती हैं। तेज़, सूखी हवाएँ बर्फ़ को उड़ा ले जाती हैं, इसलिए ज़मीन का बड़ा हिस्सा नंगी चट्टान और बजरी है। नासा ने यहाँ अपने उपकरण परखे हैं, क्योंकि यह जगह कुछ-कुछ मंगल जैसी है। यहाँ आने वाले ज़्यादातर लोग वैज्ञानिक होते हैं, जिन्हें शोध केंद्रों से हेलिकॉप्टर से लाया जाता है।

2015 में वैज्ञानिकों ने हिमनद के ऊपर रडार उड़ाया और उसके नीचे खारे पानी का एक पूरा जाल पाया, जो झरने को पानी देता है। और सबसे अजीब बात? धरती पर दूसरी जगहों पर नमक पसंद करने वाले सूक्ष्मजीव इतना ही रंगीन काम करते हैं, पूरी की पूरी झीलों को चटक गुलाबी बना देते हैं, जैसा [[@earth-weird-pink-lakes|गुलाबी झीलों]] की कहानी में है।

text: Deep under the Pacific Ocean there is a *hot spot*, a place where hot rock rises from deep [[@inside-earth|inside Earth]]. Melted rock punches up through the sea floor and piles up as volcanoes. Over hundreds of thousands of years, they grow tall enough to break the surface as islands.

st.reveal: The Pacific plate slides north-west over a fixed hot spot. Older islands are carried away north-west, while new ones form in the south-east, right over the hot spot.

You'll get a line of dots. The first dot you made has travelled farthest, just like Hawaii's oldest islands.
myth: Hawaii's volcanoes sit on the edge of a plate, like most volcanoes.
Most volcanoes do form at plate edges, but Hawaii is in the middle of the Pacific plate, thousands of kilometres from any edge. It is fed by a hot spot rising from deep below.
facts: Length of the whole volcano chain

sec.t:
The sea floor is part of the Pacific [[plate|plate]], which slides north-west by about 7 to 10 cm a year, a little faster than your fingernails grow. The hot spot stays put. So each volcano is slowly carried away, and a new one forms over the hot spot.

That is why Hawaii is a chain of islands: the oldest in the north-west, the youngest (the Big Island) in the south-east. A brand-new island is growing underwater right now.

The chain doesn't stop at the islands you see on a map. A line of drowned volcanoes, called seamounts, stretches about 6,000 km across the Pacific, almost to Russia. The oldest are around 80 million years old. Halfway along, the line bends sharply. That bend shows the plate changed direction about 47 million years ago.

Once a volcano drifts off the hot spot, it stops erupting. Then [[@cliffs-erosion|rain, waves and wind]] start wearing it down. The heavy island also slowly sinks, pressing down on the plate beneath it.

So the islands tell a life story. The Big Island is young, tall and still growing. Maui is a bit older. Kauaʻi, far to the north-west, is older still, carved by rain into steep green cliffs. Beyond it, the old volcanoes have sunk until only [[@coral-reefs|coral]] reefs and tiny [[atoll|atolls]] are left at the surface.

Kīlauea, on the Big Island, is one of the most active volcanoes in the world. It erupted almost without stopping from 1983 to 2018. Its [[lava|lava]] is runny, so it usually flows rather than explodes, and you can sometimes watch it from a safe distance. In 2018, lava flows destroyed hundreds of homes in the Puna district.

In Hawaiian tradition, Pele is the goddess of volcanoes and fire, said to live in the [[crater|crater]] of Kīlauea. Many people on the island still leave offerings and speak of her with respect.

About 35 km off the Big Island's south-east coast, a new volcano called Kamaʻehuakanaloa is growing on the sea floor. It used to be called Lōʻihi. Its top is still about 1,000 m below the surface. If it keeps growing, it may rise above the waves in tens of thousands of years.

India also rode a moving plate, all the way from near Antarctica to Asia.

text: A nuclear power plant boils water, just like a coal power plant. The difference is how it makes the heat. Instead of burning fuel, it splits [[atom|atoms]] of uranium.

The centre of a uranium-235 atom, its [[nucleus|nucleus]], is big and a little unstable. When a tiny particle called a neutron hits it, the nucleus can split into two smaller pieces. This is called fission. It releases a burst of heat and two or three more neutrons. Those neutrons can split more uranium atoms, which release more neutrons, and so on. That's a chain reaction.
In a reactor, the heat from this chain reaction warms water to make steam. The steam spins a [[turbine|turbine]], and the turbine spins a generator that makes electricity.

myth: The big towers at nuclear power plants pour out radioactive smoke.

Those are cooling towers, and the white clouds are water vapour, like steam from a kettle. They cool water from the steam side of the plant, which never touches the reactor core. Coal plants use the same kind of tower.

sec.t:
A power reactor must never let its chain reaction run away. Control rods, made of materials that soak up neutrons, slide in and out of the fuel. Push them in and the reaction slows. Pull them out and it speeds up. Huge flows of water carry heat away and keep the core cool.

The fuel itself comes as small ceramic pellets, each about the size of a fingertip, packed into long metal tubes. A single pellet can release roughly as much energy as a tonne of coal. Thick steel and concrete walls surround the reactor to hold in [[radiation|radiation]].

sec.h: Nuclear power in India and the USA
sec.t:
[[@homi-bhabha|Homi Bhabha]] founded India's atomic energy programme in the 1940s and 1950s. India's first nuclear power station opened at Tarapur, on the coast north of Mumbai, in 1969. Today India runs over 20 reactors, and plans more, but they make only about 3% of its electricity.

The USA has more nuclear reactors than any other country, over 90 of them. Together they make close to a fifth of American electricity.

Nuclear plants run day and night in any weather and give off almost no [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], the main gas warming our planet. That's why some people see them as part of the answer to [[@climate-change|climate change]].

They also have serious risks. Accidents at Chernobyl in the Soviet Union in 1986 and at Fukushima in Japan in 2011 forced many thousands of people to leave their homes. Used fuel stays dangerously [[radioactive|radioactive]] for thousands of years, and countries are still working out where to store it safely. Its slow fading is described by its [[@half-life|half-life]]. New plants are also very expensive and slow to build.

Scientists are also trying to master [[@future-energy|fusion]], joining small atoms together the way the [[@sun-what|Sun]] does. If it works, it could one day give power with far less long-lived waste.

text: लियोनार्दो दा विंची (1452–1519) इटली के चित्रकार, [[engineer|इंजीनियर]] और वैज्ञानिक थे। वे [[@renaissance|रेनेसाँ]] यानी पुनर्जागरण के दौर में रहे, जब इटली के कलाकार और विचारक प्राचीन ज्ञान को फिर से खोज रहे थे और दुनिया को नई नज़र से देख रहे थे।

उन्होंने *मोना लीसा* और *द लास्ट सपर* बनाईं, जो धरती की दो सबसे जानी-मानी पेंटिंग हैं। फिर भी उन्होंने बहुत कम पेंटिंग पूरी कीं। उनकी ज़्यादातर ऊर्जा कॉपियों में गई: हज़ारों पन्ने, पक्षियों, पानी, रोशनी, पौधों, मशीनों और इंसानी शरीर के चित्रों और विचारों से भरे हुए। वे समझना चाहते थे कि हर चीज़ कैसे काम करती है, और मानते थे कि इसे जानने का सबसे अच्छा तरीका है उसका चित्र बनाना।

sec.t:
लियोनार्दो का जन्म 1452 में तोस्काना (टस्कनी) के एक छोटे पहाड़ी कस्बे विंची के पास हुआ। उनके माता-पिता की शादी नहीं हुई थी, इसलिए वे पिता की तरह वकालत जैसे इज़्ज़तदार पेशे में नहीं जा सकते थे। आगे चलकर यही बात उनके लिए किस्मत वाली साबित हुई।

किशोर उम्र में उन्हें फ़्लोरेंस भेजा गया, ताकि वे उस समय के बड़े कलाकार आंद्रेया देल वेरोक्यो की कार्यशाला में सीख सकें। वहाँ उन्होंने पेंटिंग, [[@sculpture|मूर्तिकला]], धातु का काम और रंग पीसना सीखा। एक मशहूर किस्सा है कि जब नौजवान लियोनार्दो ने वेरोक्यो की एक तस्वीर में एक फ़रिश्ता बनाया, तो वह इतना अच्छा था कि उनके गुरु दंग रह गए।

लियोनार्दो लगभग हर जगह एक कॉपी साथ रखते थे। हज़ारों पन्ने बचे हैं, हालाँकि इससे कहीं ज़्यादा खो गए। वे दाएँ से बाएँ, उल्टी लिखावट में लिखते थे, और वे [[@left-handed|बाएँ हाथ से काम करने वाले]] थे।

पन्ने एक विषय से दूसरे पर कूदते रहते हैं। उड़ने वाली मशीन का एक खाका उन नोटों के बगल में बैठा है जिनमें लिखा है कि पानी [[vortex|भँवर]] कैसे बनाता है। उन्होंने हवा में उठने के लिए घूमने वाला एक पेंच बनाया, जो बहुत-से लोगों को [[@helicopters|हेलिकॉप्टर]] की याद दिलाता है। अपने मालिक शासकों के लिए उन्होंने [[@bridges|पुलों]], नहरों और हथियारों की योजनाएँ बनाईं। बहुत-से विचार कभी बने ही नहीं, और कुछ बनते भी तो काम न करते।

लियोनार्दो जानना चाहते थे कि खाल के नीचे क्या है। कई सालों तक उन्होंने इंसानी शवों की चीर-फाड़ की, यानी उन्हें सावधानी से खोलकर देखा। ये ज़्यादातर अस्पतालों में मरे लोगों के शव थे। जो कुछ मिला, उसके उन्होंने चित्र बनाए। हड्डियों, [[@muscles|मांसपेशियों]] और दिल के उनके चित्र अपने ज़माने के किसी भी दूसरे काम से ज़्यादा सटीक थे। यह असल में [[anatomy|शरीर-रचना]] का गहरा अध्ययन था।

उन्होंने बारीकी से देखा कि दिल के वाल्व कैसे खुलते और बंद होते हैं, और बहते खून के भँवर बनाए। आज के डॉक्टर इन चित्रों को देखते हैं तो हैरान रह जाते हैं कि उन्होंने कितना कुछ सही समझा था। अफ़सोस, ये चित्र उनकी कॉपियों में ही छिपे रहे और सदियों तक छपे नहीं, इसलिए उनके अपने समय में इनसे चिकित्सा को कोई मदद नहीं मिली।

1516 में फ़्रांस के राजा फ़्रांस्वा प्रथम ने लियोनार्दो को फ़्रांस बुलाया और आँबुआज़ के शाही किले के पास उन्हें एक घर दिया। वे *मोना लीसा* अपने साथ ले गए और उस पर काम करते रहे। 1519 में वहीं उनका निधन हुआ।

उनकी कॉपियाँ बाद में बँट गईं और बिखर गईं। उनमें से एक, कोडेक्स लेस्टर, 1994 में बिल गेट्स ने खरीदी। ये पन्ने आज भी एक ऐसे दिमाग को दिखाते हैं जिसने सवाल पूछना कभी बंद नहीं किया।

text: People began counting long before they could write. The earliest clues are bones with rows of scratched notches, perhaps used as tally marks. Later, farmers in the Middle East used small clay tokens to stand for sheep, jars of oil or bags of grain.

Around 5,000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, began pressing number signs into clay tablets. That was one of the first steps towards writing itself. Different cultures found many other ways to count, using [[@maths-binary-fingers|fingers]], body parts, knotted strings and pebbles. The number words you use today are the end of a very long story.

st.reveal: They used khipu, bundles of cords with knots. The kind and position of each knot showed ones, tens, hundreds and more. Officials used them to record taxes, harvests and people.

myth: Animals and babies have no sense of number until they are taught.

Experiments show that babies, crows, bees, fish and many other animals can tell small amounts apart, like two from three. Counting large numbers exactly, using words or symbols, is the part humans invented.

sec.t:
In 1950, a Belgian scientist digging near Ishango, close to Lake Edward in Central Africa, found a small bone with a piece of quartz fixed in one end. It is about 20,000 years old. Down its sides run groups of notches.

Some researchers think the marks are a tally, a simple record where one cut means one thing. Some see patterns in the numbers. Others say the marks might be decoration or a better grip. Nobody can be sure. But the idea of a tally is easy to understand. It is the same as a cricket scorer marking strokes on paper, or prisoners in old films counting days on a wall.

sec.h: Clay tokens and the first writing

sec.t:
Fingers are the most handy counting tool, which is why so many people count in tens. Some cultures went further. The Oksapmin of Papua New Guinea traditionally count using 27 body parts. In many parts of India and the Middle East, people count to 12 on one hand by touching the thumb to finger sections. Some historians think this may help explain the dozen.

In South America, [[@peru|the Inca]] kept records on khipu, bundles of coloured cords with [[@knots-maths|knots]]. A knot's position showed ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. Trained record-keepers could read [[@census|census]] numbers and tax records from them. Hundreds of khipu survive in museums today, and researchers are still trying to work out whether some of them also recorded words.

The Babylonians of Mesopotamia counted in groups of 60. Sixty divides neatly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, which made sharing easy. We still use their system every day: 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 360 degrees in a circle.

Over many centuries, people found faster ways to calculate, from pebbles and counting boards to the [[@abacus|abacus]]. The biggest leap came in India, with ten digits and a [[@place-value|place-value system]], where a digit's position tells you its size. To see why that worked so well, read about [[@number-systems|number systems]].

text: Spacecraft and [[@satellites-help|satellites]] have a packing problem. A rocket's nose is only a few metres wide, but [[@solar-panels|solar panels]], sunshields and antennas often need to be much bigger. They have to travel folded and open out once they are in space.

Origami, the Japanese art of folding paper, turns out to be full of maths that solves this. Engineers study how creases meet, which folds open easily and which jam. Then they design panels that fold flat into a small bundle and spread out again with a single pull, with no tearing and no tangles.

sec.h: The fold that opens in one move
sec.t:
Around 1980, the Japanese astrophysicist Koryo Miura worked out a clever pattern of slanted, zigzag creases. A sheet folded this way collapses into a neat little block. Pull two opposite corners and the whole thing [[@springs|springs]] open in one smooth motion. Push them together and it folds up again. The trick is that the creases are not at right angles. Each zigzag is slightly tilted, so all the panels move together like one piece.

It is now called the Miura fold. In 1995, Japan launched a science satellite called the Space Flyer Unit with a solar panel folded in this pattern. Some city maps in Japan are folded the same way, so they open with one tug instead of a wrestling match.

The [[@webb-telescope|James Webb Space Telescope]], launched in 2021, has to stay extremely cold to see faint heat from distant [[galaxy|galaxies]]. It is protected by a sunshield made of five thin layers, each about the size of a [[@tennis|tennis]] court.

That is far too big for any rocket. So engineers folded the sunshield and the telescope's 6.5-metre gold mirror to fit inside the nose of an Ariane 5 rocket. After launch, the telescope unfolded itself over about two weeks, using hundreds of moving parts. Each fold had been planned and tested on Earth many times.

Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory have also tested an origami-style design for a "starshade". It would be a giant flower-shaped screen, flown far in front of a telescope, to block a star's glare so that faint planets around it could be seen.

{{story:webb-telescope}}

Unfold any flat origami model and look at the creases. They follow strict rules. At any point where creases meet, the number of "mountain" folds and "valley" folds always differs by exactly two. This is called Maekawa's theorem, after the Japanese mathematician Jun Maekawa.

There is also a rule about angles. Go round the point and add up every other angle between the creases. For the model to fold flat, those angles must add up to 180 degrees.

The American physicist Robert Lang left his job with [[@lasers|lasers]] to design origami full time. He has helped engineers plan folding telescope lenses and even [[@airbags|airbags]], using the same rules.

[[@puzzle-folding-paper-moon|Every fold doubles the thickness]]. After 7 folds you have 128 layers. After 10 folds you have over 1,000. Soon the paper is thicker than it is wide and refuses to bend. If you could somehow fold an ordinary sheet 42 times, the stack would reach past the Moon.

People used to say seven folds was the limit. In 2002, Britney Gallivan, a high-school student in California, worked out a formula for how long a strip must be to fold it a given number of times. Then she proved it. Using a strip of thin paper more than a kilometre long, she folded it in half 12 times. The doubling that stopped her is the same reason [[@big-numbers|big numbers]] grow so fast.

text: The crusty or sticky stuff in the corners of your eyes in the morning is called rheum, though most people call it "sleep". It is a mix of [[mucus|mucus]], oil, dead skin cells and dust. Your eyes make these things all day to keep themselves clean and wet.

When you are awake, every [[@blinking|blink]] sweeps the mess towards the inner corner, where a tiny drain carries tears away. When you sleep, the blinking stops. The gunk collects in the corners and dries out, and by morning it is waiting for you.

st.prompt: Why does eye gunk pile up mostly while you are asleep?

options.t: You stop blinking, so nothing sweeps it away
Your eyes make extra gunk only at night
Dust falls into your eyes more at night

d.try: Sit with a friend and count how many times they blink in one minute while chatting. Then count again while they read a book or watch a screen. Most people blink far less when they concentrate, which is one reason eyes feel dry after a long time on a screen.
myth: Eye gunk is just dried-up tears.
Tears are mostly water, which evaporates. What stays behind is mostly mucus and oil, mixed with dead skin cells and dust that your eyes cleaned off during the day.

sec.t:
The surface of your eye is covered by a thin film of [[@eyes-tears|tears]], only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick. It has three layers. The inner one is sticky mucus, which helps the film cling to the eye. The middle one is mostly salty water. The outer one is oil.

That oil comes from [[gland|glands]] along the edges of your eyelids, several dozen of them, lined up like the teeth of a comb. Without the oil, your tears would dry out in seconds, the way a puddle shrinks on a hot pavement.

sec.h: A cleaning crew that never stops
sec.t:
Your eye is always under attack, from dust, [[pollen|pollen]], smoke and germs. Mucus traps these bits like flypaper. Dead cells from the surface of the eye are shed and replaced too.

Awake, you blink about 15 to 20 times a minute, more than 10,000 times a day. Each blink acts like a car's windscreen wiper. It spreads fresh tears, then pushes the dirty ones towards the inner corner. There, two small holes, one on each lid, drain the tears into a tube that runs to your nose. That is why your nose runs when you cry.

At night, the wipers stop. Mucus and oil drift to the corners and sit there for hours. The water in them evaporates, and what is left hardens into yellowish crusts or stays as soft, sticky blobs. It is the same reason [[@gross-snot|snot]] dries into crusts inside your nose.

Babies often have extra gunk, because the tiny drain from the eye to the nose can be partly blocked for the first months of life. It usually opens up on its own.

Some mornings bring more than others. A dusty room, a cold, hay fever or a long cry before bed can all mean extra gunk.

{{story:soap-germs}}

A little gunk every morning is normal and healthy. But sometimes an eye turns red, itchy or sore, with thick green or yellow gunk, or lids glued shut in the morning. That can be conjunctivitis, an [[infection|infection]] or irritation of the thin skin over the eye. It is common in children and spreads easily. Tell a parent or doctor, wash your hands often, and don't share towels.

The best way to clean gunk is with clean fingers or a damp cloth, wiping gently from the inner corner outwards. Rubbing hard can scratch the eye.

For hundreds of years, European parents told children that a figure called the Sandman sprinkled sand in their eyes to make them sleepy. The gritty crusts in the morning were said to be his leftover sand. The story appears in tales by the German writer E. T. A. Hoffmann and the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen.

Many animals get eye gunk too. Dogs and cats often have a little at the corners after a nap. And while your eyes tidy themselves overnight, the rest of you is busy too: [[@sleep-why|sleep]] is when your body repairs itself and your brain files away the day's memories.

text: Posture is the way you hold your body when you sit, stand or move. A comfortable posture lets your bones carry your weight while your muscles work without straining.

It matters, but perhaps not quite in the way you have often been told. Doctors used to think there was one correct way to sit or stand. Newer research suggests the most important thing is not to stay frozen in any position for too long. Bodies like to move. Getting up, stretching and changing position often seem to help more than sitting perfectly straight.

sec.t:
Your spine is a stack of 33 bones called vertebrae. Some at the bottom are fused together, so an adult has 24 that move. Between them sit rubbery discs that act as shock absorbers.

Seen from the side, a healthy spine isn't straight. It has three gentle curves, in the neck, upper back and lower back, making a soft S shape. These curves work like a spring, helping you absorb bumps when you walk, run and jump.

Through the day, the weight of your body slowly squeezes water out of the discs. [[@body-weird-facts|You lose about a centimetre of height by evening]], and get it back overnight while you lie down.

[[@life-school-bags|Heavy school bags]] are a worry for parents in both India and the USA. In 2020, India's government issued a School Bag Policy recommending that bags weigh no more than about 10% of a child's body weight. It also suggested that the youngest children in pre-primary classes carry no bag at all.

Wearing a backpack on both shoulders spreads the load evenly. Packing the heaviest books closest to your back helps too. If your back hurts after carrying your bag, tell a parent or teacher.

Good posture is held up by muscles, especially those in your back, belly and hips, often called your core. People who run, swim, [[@sport-climbing|climb]] or dance tend to find comfortable posture easier.

Some activities train posture on purpose. [[@ballet|Ballet]] dancers practise standing tall for hours. [[@yoga-science|Yoga]] includes poses like tadasana, the mountain pose, which is all about standing balanced and still, and many people find that [[@ayurveda-yoga|yoga]] helps them feel looser.

Astronauts aboard the International Space Station can grow up to about 5 cm taller, because their spinal discs spread out without [[@what-if-gravity-doubled|gravity pressing down]]. Some report backaches as a result. When they return to Earth, they shrink back to normal, as explained in [[@space-body|space and the body]]. [[gravity|Gravity]], it turns out, shapes our posture every moment of the day.

text: In February 1896, the French scientist Henri Becquerel was testing an idea. He thought uranium salts might soak up sunlight and then give off invisible rays. His plan was to put the salts on a photographic plate wrapped in thick black paper, leave it in the sun, and see whether the plate darkened.

Paris turned grey and cloudy, so he shoved everything into a drawer and waited. A few days later, for reasons he never fully explained, he developed the plate anyway. It was strongly fogged, with the shape of the salts clearly visible. The uranium had been giving off rays in the dark, all by itself. That property was later named radioactivity.

options.t: Bright sunlight
Electricity
A magnet

st.reveal: Becquerel thought sunlight made uranium give off rays. When the cloudy weather stopped his test, he developed the plate anyway and found it was fogged. The uranium was giving off rays all on its own, with no sunlight at all.

myth: Radioactive things glow green, like in cartoons.

Most radioactive materials don't glow at all. Radium salts do give off a faint bluish glow, and old watch dials glowed because radium was mixed with a special paint. The green glow in films is mostly made up.

sec.t:
At first, few people cared about Becquerel's rays. X-rays seemed more exciting. Then a young Polish-born scientist in Paris, [[@marie-curie|Marie Curie]], picked uranium rays as the topic for her doctorate in 1897.

She found that the strength of the rays depended only on how much uranium was present, not on whether it was hot, cold, wet or powdered. That meant the rays were coming from inside the [[atom|atoms]] themselves. It was a shocking idea at the time, when many people thought atoms could never change.

With her husband Pierre, she ground up and boiled tonnes of a black ore called pitchblende in a leaky shed. In 1898 they found two new [[element|elements]]. One they named polonium, after Marie's homeland, Poland. The other, radium, was about a million times more [[radioactive|radioactive]] than uranium. They also coined the word "radioactivity".

In 1903, Becquerel and both Curies shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. In 1911 Marie won a second Nobel, in chemistry, making her the first person to win two.

Nobody yet understood the danger. Pierre carried radium in his pocket, and Becquerel once got a burn on his skin from a tube of it in his waistcoat. Marie's health was harmed by years of work with radioactive substances. Her lab notebooks, even her cookbook, are still radioactive today. Researchers who want to read them must wear protective clothing and sign a form.

sec.h: From a drawer to the world
sec.t:
Radioactivity changed medicine, energy and our picture of the Earth. Doctors use it to treat cancer and to make images of the body. [[@nuclear-power|Nuclear power]] stations make electricity from atoms splitting apart. India's atomic research, started by [[@homi-bhabha|Homi Bhabha]] in the 1940s, grew from this science.

There is also a slow, steady clock hidden inside radioactive atoms. Each kind breaks down at its own fixed pace, measured by its [[@half-life|half-life]]. Measuring how much is left tells scientists the age of ancient bones, rocks and even the Earth itself, which turns out to be about 4.5 billion years old.

text: The first true battery was invented by the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta around 1799. He stacked discs of zinc and copper or silver, with pieces of cloth or cardboard soaked in salty water between each pair. When he connected the top and bottom of the stack with a wire, a steady electric current flowed. He described it in a letter to the Royal Society in London in 1800.

Before Volta, scientists could only make [[@electricity-made|electricity]] in short sparks, by [[@static-electricity|rubbing things together]]. His "pile" gave a continuous flow for the first time. Every battery since, from torch cells to the lithium battery in a phone, works on his basic idea: two different materials and a chemical between them.

st.reveal: Galvani believed living bodies made their own electricity. Alessandro Volta disagreed. He suspected the two metals, with something wet between them, were making the current. To prove it, he built a stack of metal discs with no frog at all, and it worked. That stack was the first battery.

These clay jars, about 2,000 years old, contained a copper tube and an iron rod, and some people have claimed they made electricity. No wires or electrical devices have ever been found with them. Most archaeologists think they were simply used to store scrolls or other objects.

sec.t:
In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani, a doctor in Bologna, was studying [[@frogs-monsoon|frogs]]. He noticed that a dead frog's leg twitched when he touched it with two different metals at once. Galvani decided the frog's body must contain "animal electricity".

Volta, a physics professor in Pavia, was not convinced. He thought the electricity came from the two metals touching the wet frog, and the leg simply reacted to it. The two men argued politely through letters and papers for years. To settle it, Volta built his pile with no animal at all. It made electricity. In a way, both were partly right: [[@nervous-system|our nerves]] really do use electrical signals, which Galvani had spotted.

Volta's pile ran down and couldn't be refilled. In 1859, the French physicist Gaston Planté invented the lead-acid battery, which could be recharged by pushing current back through it. Updated versions still start most petrol cars and back up inverters in Indian homes during [[@what-if-no-electricity|power cuts]].

In 1866, the French engineer Georges Leclanché invented a cell that later developed into the "dry cell", with a paste instead of a liquid. That made batteries safe to carry around and led to the torch batteries and AA cells you know today.

In the 1970s, an English chemist working in the USA, Stanley Whittingham, built a battery using lithium, a very light metal. It was powerful but could catch fire. John Goodenough, working in Oxford, found a better material for one side of the battery in 1980. In 1985, Akira Yoshino in Japan made a safer, practical version. Sony began selling lithium-ion batteries in 1991.

[[@batteries-future|Lithium-ion batteries]] are light and hold a lot of energy, and they can be recharged hundreds of times. They made mobile phones, laptops and [[@electric-cars|electric cars]] possible. In 2019, the three scientists shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Goodenough was 97.

Batteries also store power from [[@solar-panels|solar panels]] for use at night, a big part of plans for cleaner energy. And Volta's name is printed on every one, in the little "V" on the label.

text: The Colosseum was a giant stadium in the centre of Rome where crowds came to watch shows put on by the emperor. The most famous were [[@gladiators|gladiator fights]], in which trained fighters battled each other with swords, spears, nets and shields. There were also hunts of wild animals brought from across the [[empire|empire]], and public executions of criminals.

The shows were free. Emperors used them to win popularity, to show off the empire's reach and to keep the people of Rome entertained. A day at the games could run from morning hunts to afternoon gladiator bouts.

st.prompt: How did the Colosseum keep about 50,000 spectators out of the hot sun?

A glass roof
Tall trees planted around the top

st.reveal: A giant canvas awning called the velarium was stretched over the seats on ropes and wooden poles. Sailors from the Roman navy, who knew how to handle sails and rigging, are said to have worked it. It probably covered the seats but left the arena open.

myth: In the Colosseum, thumbs down meant "kill the gladiator" and thumbs up meant "let him live".

Roman writers mention a "turned thumb" but do not say which way it turned. The thumbs-down idea became famous from a painting by Jean-Léon Gérôme in 1872. Some historians think a hidden thumb, pressed into the fist, may have meant mercy.

sec.t:
The Colosseum's real name was the Flavian Amphitheatre, after the family of emperors who built it. Emperor Vespasian began it around 70 CE, on land where the unpopular emperor Nero had built a private lake. His son Titus opened it in 80 CE with 100 days of games.

It was built with stone, brick and Roman concrete, on four storeys of arches. About 50,000 people could fit inside. That is fewer than at a big cricket ground today: the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad holds more than twice as many. But no stadium of its time came close.

The Colosseum had 80 entrances at ground level, and most were numbered. Spectators carried tokens telling them which entrance, section and row to use. Passages called vomitoria let the crowd pour out quickly, so a full stadium could empty fast.

Seats were arranged by rank. Senators sat closest to the arena, ordinary men higher up, and women and the poor at the very top. Over the seats, sailors handled a huge canvas awning on ropes to block the sun.

Most gladiators were enslaved people, prisoners of war or condemned criminals. A few were free men who signed up for money and fame. They trained in schools next to the Colosseum and fought in set styles: one with a net and trident, another with a sword and big shield. Popular gladiators were celebrities, painted on walls and scratched in [[@oddity-ancient-graffiti|graffiti]].

Not every fight ended in death. Gladiators were expensive to train, and many bouts ended when one fighter gave up. The crowd and the emperor then decided whether the loser would be spared.

Animal hunts brought lions, leopards, bears, ostriches and [[@elephants-talk|elephants]] from Africa and Asia. Thousands of animals died in the games over the years. Today most people find these shows cruel, and a few Romans, such as the philosopher Seneca, wrote that the bloodshed disgusted them.

{{story:pulleys}}

Under the wooden arena floor, covered with sand, lay the hypogeum: two storeys of [[@tunnels|tunnels]], cages and machinery, added by Emperor Domitian. Workers turned capstans, upright winding drums, to haul cages up on ropes and [[@pulleys|pulleys]]. Trapdoors opened, and animals or scenery appeared in the middle of the arena. The word "arena" comes from the [[@latin-roots|Latin]] for sand, which soaked up blood and gave fighters grip.

Gladiator fights ended in the early 400s CE, and animal hunts stopped about a century later. Over the next thousand years, the Colosseum was used for housing, workshops and even as a [[fortress|fortress]]. [[@earthquakes|Earthquakes]], including a strong one in 1349, brought down part of the outer wall. People carried away the fallen stone for new buildings.

The holes you see all over its walls once held iron clamps, which were dug out and melted down. Today the Colosseum is one of the most visited monuments on Earth, a symbol of Rome, and a reminder of how a city entertained itself 2,000 years ago.

text: The Acropolis is a flat-topped hill of rock that rises in the middle of Athens, the capital of Greece. "Acropolis" means "high city" in Greek. Many ancient Greek towns had one, a safe high place for temples and a last line of defence. The one in Athens is by far the most famous.

On top stand the ruins of temples built about 2,500 years ago. The biggest is the Parthenon, a temple to Athena, the goddess of wisdom and the protector of the city. Beside it stand smaller temples, including the Erechtheion, whose porch roof is held up by six stone statues of young women instead of columns. Millions of people climb up to see it all every year, usually early in the morning, before the summer sun turns the bare rock into an oven.

st.reveal: During a war between Venice and the Ottoman Empire, the Ottoman army kept gunpowder in the Parthenon. A Venetian cannonball set it off, and the blast tore out the roof and many columns.

myth: Ancient Greek temples and statues were always plain white marble.
Many were painted in bright colours. Scientists have found traces of blue, red and gold paint on Greek sculptures. Most of it has worn away over the centuries, leaving the white stone we see today.

sec.h: Built when Athens was at its richest
sec.t:
Around 450 BCE, Athens was a powerful city. It had led other Greek cities against the Persian Empire and collected money from its allies. A leader named Pericles used some of that money to rebuild the Acropolis, which Persian soldiers had burned in 480 BCE.

The Parthenon went up between 447 and 432 BCE. The sculptor Phidias led the decoration. Inside stood a giant statue of Athena, about 12 metres tall, covered in gold and ivory. It was lost long ago, and nobody knows exactly what happened to it. Those were also the years when Athens ran an early form of [[@democracy-athens|democracy]], with male citizens voting on laws.

sec.h: A temple, a church, a mosque and a gunpowder store
sec.t:
The Parthenon has had many lives. In the centuries after ancient Greece, it became a Christian church. When the Ottoman Empire ruled Athens, it became a mosque.

In 1687, an army from Venice attacked the Ottomans in Athens. The Ottoman soldiers were storing gunpowder inside the Parthenon. On 26 September, a Venetian cannonball hit it. The explosion blew out the roof and brought down many columns. What you see today is mostly the result of that one day.

In the early 1800s, agents of a British ambassador, Lord Elgin, removed about half of the surviving Parthenon [[sculpture|sculptures]] and shipped them to Britain. He said he had permission from the Ottoman rulers. Today they are in the British Museum in London.

Greece has asked for them back for decades, and many people agree. The British Museum says it holds them legally and shows them to visitors from all over the world. In 2009, Athens opened the new Acropolis Museum at the foot of the hill. Its top floor has empty spaces left for the missing [[@sculpture|sculptures]], next to plaster copies.

Since 1975, Greek teams have been carefully repairing the Acropolis. Earlier repairs used iron clamps, which rusted, swelled and cracked the marble. Engineers are replacing them with titanium, which doesn't rust. They also use fresh marble from Mount Pentelikon, the same mountain the ancient builders quarried, so new pieces match the old.

text: The Vatican, or Vatican City, is the smallest country in the world. It covers about 0.44 square kilometres, roughly the area of 60 football fields, and sits inside the city of [[@rome-city|Rome]] in Italy, on the west bank of the river Tiber. It is the home of the pope, the leader of the Roman Catholic Church, which had about 1.4 billion members worldwide in 2023.

The Vatican has its own flag, stamps, coins, radio station and police. Fewer than 1,000 people live there, mostly priests, nuns and guards. But millions visit every year to see St Peter's Basilica, the Sistine Chapel and some of the most famous art on Earth.

st.reveal: Ballots are burned after each vote. Chemicals make the smoke black if no pope has been chosen and white if one has. Bells of St Peter's also ring for a new pope, but the smoke is the famous signal.

sec.t:
For over a thousand years, popes ruled a large area of central Italy called the Papal States. When Italy became one country in the 1800s, it took over those lands, including Rome, in 1870. The popes refused to accept it and stayed inside the Vatican for nearly 60 years.

In 1929, the Lateran Treaty between the pope and the Italian government settled the dispute. Italy recognised Vatican City as an independent country. The pope gave up any claim to the rest of the old Papal States.

sec.h: St Peter's and the Sistine Chapel
A country with a pope as king
sec.t:
The pope is the head of the Catholic Church and also the ruler of Vatican City. He is elected by cardinals, senior church leaders, in a secret meeting called a conclave held in the Sistine Chapel. The doors are locked and the cardinals vote again and again until one person gets two-thirds of the votes. A pope usually serves until he dies, though Benedict XVI chose to step down in 2013.

In May 2025, the cardinals elected Robert Prevost, born in Chicago, who took the name Leo XIV. He was the first pope from the United States, though he had spent many years working in Peru. The previous pope, Francis, came from Argentina and was the first from the Americas.

The Vatican's small army is the Pontifical Swiss Guard, founded in 1506. There are about 135 guards. They must be unmarried when they join, Catholic, Swiss citizens and men between 19 and 30. On duty at the gates, they wear striped blue, red and yellow uniforms and carry halberds, a mix of spear and axe.

Behind the old uniforms, they are trained bodyguards. The colourful clothes are for ceremonies.

The Vatican Museums hold one of the world's great art collections, gathered by popes over centuries. There are ancient Roman and Egyptian statues, maps painted on walls, and rooms decorated by the painter Raphael. On a busy day, more than 20,000 people pass through, and a full walk through the galleries is several kilometres long.

The Vatican also has a library with ancient [[manuscript|manuscripts]] and an [[observatory|observatory]], with telescopes now in Arizona, US, where its astronomers study the stars.

text: Marathi and Gujarati both grew out of older spoken languages of western India, called Prakrits and Apabhramsha, which themselves came from the same ancient roots as Sanskrit. Over hundreds of years, the way people spoke changed bit by bit, until by around a thousand years ago these had become recognisable early forms of Marathi and Gujarati.

They grew through poetry, devotional songs, trade and royal courts. Today Marathi is spoken by about 8.3 crore people and Gujarati by about 5.5 crore, according to India's 2011 Census. Both are official languages of their states, and both have large communities abroad.

st.prompt: Marathi and Hindi are both written in Devanagari. What does that tell you about the two languages?

That Marathi is a dialect of Hindi
That anyone who reads Hindi can understand Marathi easily

st.reveal: A script is only a way of writing sounds. English, French and Spanish all use the same Latin letters but are different languages. Marathi and Hindi are related, but they have different words, grammar and endings.

sec.t:
In the 1200s, much serious writing in India was in Sanskrit, which most ordinary people could not read. In 1290, a young saint named Dnyaneshwar wrote the *Dnyaneshwari*, an explanation of the [[@bhagavad-gita|Bhagavad Gita]] in Marathi verse, so that everyone could understand it. Tradition says he was only about sixteen.

Other saints followed. Tukaram, in the 1600s, wrote *abhangas*, devotional songs still sung by pilgrims who walk to the temple town of Pandharpur. In Gujarat, the poet Narsinh Mehta wrote songs to Krishna in the 1400s. One of them, *Vaishnava Jana To*, describes a good person as one who feels the pain of others. It became one of [[@gandhi|Gandhi's]] favourite hymns.

These singers belonged to the [[bhakti|bhakti]] movement, which spread devotion in everyday languages across India, much like the poems of [[@mirabai-kabir|Mirabai and Kabir]] in the north.

{{story:gandhi}}

In the 1600s, [[@shivaji|Shivaji]] made Marathi a language of government in his kingdom and had a dictionary made to replace many Persian official words with Sanskrit and Marathi ones. For centuries, Marathi letters and accounts were written in a fast, flowing script called Modi, which let a writer keep the pen on the paper. Today Marathi uses Devanagari, the same [[script|script]] as Hindi and Sanskrit.

Gujarati became the language of traders. Gujarati merchants sailed to Arabia, East Africa and Southeast Asia for centuries, and their account books were often written in a quick script without the top line. That simple, flowing style became the Gujarati script used today.

After independence, Marathi and Gujarati speakers shared a large state called Bombay State. Many people in both communities wanted their own state. The Samyukta Maharashtra movement campaigned for a Marathi state, and the Mahagujarat movement for a Gujarati one. There were long, sometimes violent protests, especially over which state should get the city of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]].

On 1 May 1960, Bombay State was divided. Maharashtra, with Mumbai as its capital, and Gujarat were created on the same day. Both states still celebrate 1 May as their foundation day. It was part of a wider redrawing of [[@states-india|India's states]] along language lines.

Gandhi wrote his [[autobiography|autobiography]], *The Story of My Experiments with Truth*, in Gujarati, in the 1920s. It was later translated into many languages. Gandhi wanted Indians to value their own mother tongues. Alongside his English weekly, *Young India*, he ran a Gujarati weekly called *Navajivan*.

In 2024, the Government of India declared Marathi a classical language. Marathi has given India a huge theatre tradition, and Mumbai's film industry was born in a Marathi-speaking city. Gujarati is now heard in shops and temples from Leicester in England to Edison, New Jersey, where many Gujarati families have settled.

text: Tea is now so Indian that it is hard to picture a railway station or a street corner without a chaiwala. Yet tea drinking became common across India only in the 20th century.

The story begins with the British. In the 1800s, Britain bought most of its tea from [[@china-today|China]], and the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] wanted a supply of its own. It set up tea gardens in [[@assam-tea|Assam]] and later in Darjeeling and the Nilgiris, at first only to sell tea to Britain. Later, when sales abroad slowed, the tea industry ran big campaigns to get Indians drinking it. Indians took the drink and made it their own, boiled with milk, sugar and spices.

myth: Green tea and black tea come from different plants.

Both come from Camellia sinensis. For black tea, the leaves are crushed and left to darken in the air before drying. For green tea, they are heated soon after picking, which stops the change and keeps them green.

sec.t:
People in China have drunk tea for well over 2,000 years. The British long believed tea grew only there. But in the 1820s, a Scottish trader named Robert Bruce learned that the Singpho people of Assam drank a brew made from a local wild tea plant. An Assamese nobleman, Maniram Dewan, helped guide him to it.

The Assam plant was a larger-leaved kind of the same [[species|species]]. In 1839, the first Assam tea was auctioned in London. Soon [[@forests-india|forests]] in the Brahmaputra valley were being cleared for tea gardens. [[@northeast-india|Northeast India]] still grows more than half of India's tea.

sec.h: The hard side of the tea garden
sec.t:
Tea needed many workers to pick leaves by hand. In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people were brought to Assam from places such as Jharkhand and Odisha on harsh contracts. Pay was low, living conditions were poor, and many people fell ill.

Their [[descendant|descendants]] still make up much of the workforce in Assam's tea gardens. Many historians now tell the tea story with them at its centre.

In the early 1900s, most Indians did not drink tea. Then the tea industry, run mostly by British planters, began promoting it, especially from the 1930s. Its stalls handed out free cups at railway stations, fairs and factories, and showed people how to brew it.

The promoters wanted a light tea with a dash of milk. Indians had other ideas. They boiled the leaves with plenty of milk and sugar and often ginger, [[@cardamom-pepper|cardamom]] or cloves. That strong, sweet [[@food-chai-history|masala chai]] became the national drink. Tea stalls on [[@indian-railways|railway platforms]] helped carry it to every corner of the country.

sec.h: Leaves, dust and a clay cup
sec.t:
Most tea grown in India is turned into small, hard grains by a method called CTC, short for crush, tear, curl. It brews quickly and strongly, which is perfect for chai. Darjeeling tea, grown high in the hills, is usually made as whole leaves and is prized around the world for its delicate taste.

In many towns, chai is still poured into a kulhad, a little unglazed clay cup that gives the tea an earthy smell. After one use, it is thrown away and crumbles back into soil.
